transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-02-17 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Alex (QR CTO), Priya (QR ML), Sam (QR SRE), Rina (QR Product)

Auto-summary: quick sync focused on latency and throughput constraints for a live streaming annotation product.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you all hear me ok?
00:05 Alex: yeah loud and clear, thanks for fitting us in, we wanted to go deep on latency/throughput — p95s mostly for streaming-output use case
00:15 Jordan: great. quick rundown from our side, Maya will cover the benchmark approach and streaming knobs, Liam can jump into deployment options later
00:25 Priya: quick context — our prod path is a short prompt (typically 40–80 tokens input) and we stream responses back to the browser. target is p95 < 120ms for single-token incremental updates, ideally hitting 90ms inside eu-west region. concurrency varies, typical steady is 200 concurrent sessions, burst to 2k for 20–60s during peak events
00:50 Maya: ok that helps. couple clarifying q's — what model sized roughly? 7B or 13B?
00:58 Priya: mostly 7B for now, evaluating 13B for more complex samples but that will be smaller % of traffic
01:05 Liam: cool. for 7B on our hosted fleet we often see token generation latency that can sat around 30–50ms per token on optimized kernels, but depends on sequence length and kv cache hit rate
01:20 Sam: when you say kv cache hit rate, do you mean session persistence? we do sticky sessions in our app but users may open new tabs and sometimes lose state
01:30 Maya: yes, exactly — if you can reuse the KV cache across tokens the runtime avoids re-computing key/values on prefix which cuts token time dramatically. for streaming p95s the key is maintaining session affinity or using prefix caching on the server side
01:45 Rina: do you have examples of p95 numbers for 7B streaming under concurrency? our concern is the burst to 2k — we can't accept 500ms spikes
01:55 Maya: typical hosted numbers for 7B with persistent sessions: p95 per-token 40–80ms at 200 concurrent. at 2k concurrent you'd need autoscaling or Dedicated pools, otherwise you'll introduce queuing and p95 jumps to 300–500ms
02:15 Jordan: so tradeoff — hosted is fastest to start, but Dedicated gives predictable pool sizing for big bursts. Private (VPC/on-prem) adds network egress and cold-start factors but gives control over infra
02:30 Alex: timeline — we have a marketing event in 6 weeks we want to be ready for. so we need a quick baseline and contingency plan in case hosted can't hold the 2k burst
02:40 Jordan: understood. propose: run a 1-week hosted baseline with your prompt set, measure steady and burst with our harness. if it fails for p95 under your burst, we propose a Dedicated proof of concept with reserved pool to validate 2k burst for 7B
02:55 Priya: sounds reasonable. what about cost? our CFO will ask. is Dedicated a lot more expensive?
03:05 Jordan: Dedicated is commit-based. cost per-token drops with efficient batching and caching but you pay for reserved GPUs. We'll provide a ballpark after the baseline; SE will include batching/quantization recommendations that reduce unit cost
03:20 Sam: network — for Private/VPC we need to keep traffic inside our VPC and have KMS for keys. any gotchas integrating your Private control plane with our HSM?
03:33 Maya: we support KMS integrations and can use customer-managed keys. Private does require some ops setup (VPN or VPC peering). HSM specifics can add time — we'd want SRE to share their HSM vendor and we can validate compatibility
03:48 Priya: on benchmarking, do you provide a harness we can run against our environment to verify numbers locally?
03:55 Liam: yes — Maya's team has a dockerized harness that simulates streaming token-by-token with session affinity, varying seq len and concurrency. we'll send the scripts and a sample postman collection to exercise the streaming endpoint
04:10 Alex: great. and we will share a canonical prompt set — about 600 unique prompts that represent 80% of traffic
04:18 Jordan: awesome. a few technical points to capture: (1) batching — continuous batching helps throughput but adds micro-latency; (2) prefilling and KV cache — for repeated prefixes it's huge win; (3) quantization — 4-bit quant helps cost but watch model quality; (4) fallback policies — if a request times out we can fall back to a smaller model
04:40 Priya: fallback sounds useful. if the model degrades in quality with quant, can we auto-fall back to a higher-precision variant?
04:48 Maya: yes, we support model variants and automatic fallback routing by policy (latency or quality). you can pin important routes to higher fidelity models while letting less critical calls use quantized variants
05:00 Sam: curious about cold starts — if a user session appears after minutes of inactivity will there be a cold kernel load that impacts that user's initial tokens?
05:10 Liam: cold starts are a factor especially in Private/on-prem. Hosted uses hot pools and pre-warmed caches so initial impact is smaller. Dedicated can be kept hot if you reserve capacity and configure keep-alives
05:25 Rina: for our SLA we define application-level p95 (end-to-end) including network time. do you have tracing hooks so we can break down where time is spent?
05:33 Maya: yes console provides per-token latency breakdown (model compute, queuing, network), and we provide trace hooks you can send to Jaeger or our tracing UI for deep dives
05:45 Alex: regarding metrics, can you also report tokens/sec and useful per-GPU concurrency so we can extrapolate costs?
05:52 Jordan: yes, the report will include tokens/sec, p95/p99, avg latency, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and cost per 1k tokens under current config
06:05 Priya: what's a realistic token/sec for 7B in streaming for a single GPU?
06:12 Maya: depends on batch shape and sequence, but roughly 300–800 tokens/sec per GPU for streaming workloads with continuous batching. with KV cache and stable short seq you may see the higher end. With 13B that drops by roughly 30–40%
06:30 Sam: if our peak is 2k concurrent sessions and average generation rate is 5 tokens/sec per session, that's 10k tokens/sec peak. how many GPUs is that roughly?
06:42 Maya: rough math: if a GPU sustains 600 tokens/sec, you'd need ~17 GPUs for steady 10k tokens/sec. accounting for autoscale headroom and failover you'd size ~22 GPUs or use Dedicated + burst pooling
07:00 Alex: ok that's useful. can Redwood provide a sizing doc and an estimate for both hosted burst mitigation and Dedicated reserved pool?
07:08 Jordan: yes we'll include both: hosted with autoscaling and pre-warmed burst policy, and Dedicated with x GPUs hot + y GPUs for burst, plus cost delta
07:20 Priya: how do you handle token-rate throttling per-tenant to avoid noisy-neighbor? we need per-customer quotas and graceful degradation
07:27 Maya: we support token-level quotas, leaky-bucket throttling, and graceful fallback to smaller models or queued responses. Console shows token-level usage per API key so you can analyze heavy users
07:40 Sam: any limitations on streaming chunk size? we stream as small as 1 token updates; do you support that low-latency pattern?
07:48 Liam: yes streaming token-by-token is supported. there are micro-batching windows (2–5ms) inside the runtime to increase throughput but we expose tunables for latency-sensitive flows
07:58 Rina: we are concerned about p95 spikes during network incidents across region. do you support multi-region failover or cross-region fallbacks?
08:06 Maya: yes, smart routing can failover to another region or to a cheaper model variant in a different region. that adds cross-region latency but keeps requests served instead of failing
08:16 Alex: competitor question — are there big differences vs Anthropic's managed endpoints for streaming?
08:22 Jordan: high level — many managed endpoints are similar for basic generation. Redwood differentiates with runtime knobs for high-throughput streaming, explicit caching, and Dedicated/private deployment options tailored to predictable bursts and compliance
08:36 Priya: ok practical next steps — we'll share prompts and topology. you will run a hosted baseline. when will we see results?
08:44 Maya: we'll kick off the harness this week once we have the prompt set. expect initial baseline results in 3 business days and a full report in 7 days
08:53 Jordan: also we should plan a Dedicated sizing session in the follow-up where we go through their traffic curve and map GPUs to cost
09:00 Sam: question — for Private deployment how long to spin up an on-prem cluster?
09:06 Liam: on-prem timeframe varies; technically 2–6 weeks depending on networking, HSM work, and validation. VPC options are faster — more like 1–2 weeks if peering and keys are ready
09:18 Priya: any pre-existing reference architecture docs for heavy streaming customers?
09:22 Jordan: yes will attach a reference playbook — includes burst strategies, keep-alives, batching parameters, and example infra diagrams
09:30 Rina: and please note our security requires SOC2 and quarterly audits — will that be in the pack?
09:35 Jordan: yes SOC2 summary and compliance artifacts will be included in the security pack
09:40 Alex: ok wrapping up — agree on baseline + security pack + sizing doc. thanks everyone
09:48 Jordan: thanks all, Maya will post harness + scripts and Jordan will follow up with pricing and next meeting invite
09:55 Priya: thanks, bye
09:58 (call ends)
